html:
"Should we use SQL or NoSQL?" comes up in every design. The honest answer starts with what your data looks like and how you read it, not with what's popular. Here are the main kinds of databases, what each does well, and how to pick.

Relational (SQL) Databases

PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle. Data lives in tables with a fixed schema, linked by keys, and you ask questions in SQL.

They're good at:

  • Relationships: customers, orders and products, joined in one query.
  • Transactions: move money between two accounts, all or nothing (ACID).
  • Constraints: unique emails, foreign keys, NOT NULL. The database refuses bad data.
  • Questions you didn't plan for: any filter, group or join, later, with an index.

Their limit: one database server takes all the writes. They scale up well, and reads scale with replicas, but spreading writes over many machines (sharding) is hard work.

NoSQL: Four Different Families

"NoSQL" isn't one thing. It's four families built for different access patterns.

Document Databases

MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore. Each record is a JSON-like document that can hold nested data, and documents in one collection can have different fields.

Good for data you read as a whole, like a product with its variants and attributes, or a user profile. Less good when you need to join across collections often.

Key-Value Stores

Redis, DynamoDB (also more than that), Memcached. A giant dictionary: give a key, get a value, in a millisecond or less.

Good for caches, sessions, counters, rate limits and shopping carts. You can only look things up by key, so plan your keys carefully.

Wide-Column Stores

Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable. Rows are grouped by a partition key and sorted within it, spread over many machines.

Good for huge write volumes: sensor data, logs, messages, activity feeds. You design the tables around the exact queries you'll run, and other queries are slow or impossible.

Graph Databases

Neo4j, Amazon Neptune. Data is nodes and the edges between them.

Good when the relationships are the point: "friends of friends who like this", fraud rings, recommendations. Overkill for everything else.

Side by Side

Need Good fit
Related data, transactions, flexible queries Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Self-contained records with varying fields Document (MongoDB)
Very fast lookups by key, caching, sessions Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB)
Massive writes, queries known in advance Wide-column (Cassandra)
Deep relationship queries Graph (Neo4j)

How to Choose

Ask these questions, in order:

  1. Do you need transactions across several records? Payments, stock, bookings: start relational.
  2. Do you know all your queries in advance? If not, relational gives you room to change your mind.
  3. Will writes outgrow one big server? Hundreds of thousands of writes per second, all the time: consider wide-column or a sharded store.
  4. Is it mostly lookups by one key? A key-value store, often as a cache in front of the main database.

For most applications, the answer is a relational database, plus Redis as a cache. Modern PostgreSQL also stores and indexes JSON (jsonb), so "my data has some flexible fields" isn't a reason to leave it.

Many real systems use several: PostgreSQL for orders, Redis for sessions, Elasticsearch for search, and a wide-column store for the activity feed. That's called polyglot persistence: each kind of data in the store that suits it.

Myths to Drop

  • "NoSQL is faster." It's faster for the access pattern it was built for, and slower or impossible for others.
  • "NoSQL has no schema." The schema moves into your code, and you still have to handle old and new shapes of data.
  • "SQL doesn't scale." Large companies run huge PostgreSQL and MySQL fleets. It scales with more effort for writes.

The Answer in Short

  1. Relational databases give you relationships, transactions, constraints and flexible queries.
  2. NoSQL is four families: document, key-value, wide-column and graph, each for one access pattern.
  3. Choose from your data and your queries: transactions and unknown queries mean SQL; massive writes on known queries can mean wide-column.
  4. The usual default: PostgreSQL plus Redis.
  5. Using several databases for different data is normal.
